blocks.text: 1. Bayesian Optimization

blocks.alt: Past trials feed a surrogate model that produces a smarter next guess

blocks.text: Grid Search and Random Search, the two previous topics, both share a quiet, structural limitation: every combination they evaluate is chosen ahead of time, or purely at random, with absolutely no use made of the results already gathered from previous evaluations to inform where to look next. Bayesian Optimization does something genuinely different, using the results of every past evaluation to intelligently, deliberately decide exactly where to sample next.

This directly echoes a probabilistic philosophy already covered twice in this course, once for Gaussian Mixture Models in the Clustering Algorithms module, and once for Bayesian Regression in the Regression module, both of which treated unknown quantities as probability distributions to be refined with evidence, rather than single fixed values. Bayesian Optimization applies that exact same philosophy directly to the hyperparameter search problem itself.
2. The Core Idea

blocks.alt: Trying a point, learning from the result, and picking a better next point

blocks.text: Bayesian Optimization treats the relationship between a model's hyperparameters and its cross validation score as an unknown function, one that is genuinely expensive to evaluate at any single point, since evaluating it even once requires fully training and cross validating a model. Rather than exploring this unknown function blindly, Bayesian Optimization builds a probabilistic model that estimates what this unknown function likely looks like, based on whatever evaluations have already been observed.

This probabilistic model is then used directly to decide which untried hyperparameter combination is most worth evaluating next, that combination is actually evaluated, the probabilistic model is updated with this new real result, and the entire cycle repeats. Each successive round makes the underlying probabilistic model a bit more accurate, and each successive choice of where to sample next becomes correspondingly better informed than the one before it.
3. The Surrogate Model

blocks.alt: A real, expensive objective is approximated by a cheap surrogate model

blocks.text: The probabilistic model Bayesian Optimization builds is called a surrogate model, since it stands in as a cheap, fast approximation for the true, expensive relationship between hyperparameters and performance, one that would otherwise require a full, costly training and cross validation run to check at any single point.

The most common choice of surrogate model is a Gaussian Process, a probabilistic modeling technique closely related to the Gaussian distributions already covered in depth for Gaussian Mixture Models, extended here to model an entire unknown function rather than just a fixed set of data points. This surrogate model gets refit after every single real evaluation, growing progressively more accurate and more informative as more genuine evaluations accumulate over the course of the search.
4. Predicted Score and Uncertainty

A key property of the Gaussian Process surrogate model is that it provides two distinct pieces of information at every single point in the hyperparameter search space, not just one. First, a predicted score, the surrogate's best current guess at how well that specific hyperparameter combination would actually perform if evaluated. Second, an uncertainty estimate, a measure of exactly how confident the surrogate actually is in that particular guess.

A region with a high predicted score looks genuinely promising based on the evidence gathered so far. A region with high uncertainty, by contrast, has barely been explored at all, meaning it could hide either a disappointing result or a genuinely pleasant surprise, information the surrogate simply does not have enough evidence to resolve yet. Both of these pieces of information, predicted score and uncertainty, together drive the crucial decision covered in the next section.
5. Balancing Exploration and Exploitation

blocks.alt: Exploring new areas is balanced against exploiting the best known area

blocks.text: Deciding where to sample next requires balancing two competing strategies. Exploitation means sampling near whichever point has scored best so far, refining and confirming a promising region the search has already identified. Exploration means instead sampling in a genuinely uncertain, largely unexplored region of the search space, on the chance that it might hide something even better than anything found so far.

Leaning too heavily toward exploitation risks the search settling prematurely on a merely good, local optimum, entirely missing a genuinely better region elsewhere in the space that was never adequately explored. Leaning too heavily toward exploration wastes evaluations, an expensive resource by assumption, on regions that ultimately turn out to be genuinely unpromising. A well-designed Bayesian Optimization search deliberately balances both of these competing strategies rather than committing fully to either one.

blocks.text: 6. The Acquisition Function

blocks.alt: The surrogate model feeds an acquisition function that picks the next point to try

blocks.text: The mechanism that actually balances exploration against exploitation is called the acquisition function, which combines the surrogate model's predicted score and uncertainty estimate, both already covered in the previous two sections, into a single ranking number for every point in the search space.

Expected Improvement is a common, standard choice of acquisition function, ranking every untried point by how much it is genuinely expected to beat the best result found anywhere so far, a calculation that naturally rewards both a high predicted score, exploitation, and high uncertainty, exploration, since either one can plausibly lead to genuine improvement over the current best. Whichever point the acquisition function ranks highest is the one that actually gets evaluated next, closing the loop already covered in the Core Idea section.
7. Reaching Good Results with Fewer Evaluations

Grid Search and Random Search, both covered in the previous two topics, treat every single evaluation as entirely independent, learning absolutely nothing from past results that could inform future choices. Bayesian Optimization, by directly using every single past result to inform the very next choice, exactly the mechanism covered throughout this topic, often reaches a comparably good, or even better, final result using dramatically fewer total evaluations than either of those two simpler approaches would require.

This sample efficiency advantage becomes especially valuable whenever each individual evaluation is itself genuinely expensive, training a large, complex deep learning model that takes hours to complete being a classic example, since Bayesian Optimization's smarter, informed choices can meaningfully reduce the total number of these expensive evaluations needed to find a genuinely good hyperparameter setting.
8. A Real Cost: Sequential, Hard-to-Parallelize Structure

It is worth connecting this directly back to the sequential dependency already covered in depth for Boosting in the Ensemble Learning module. Bayesian Optimization shares that exact same structural property: every single step genuinely, mathematically depends on the results of every step that came before it, since the surrogate model must be updated with each new evaluation before the acquisition function can meaningfully decide where to look next.

This sequential dependency means Bayesian Optimization cannot be trivially parallelized across many machines simultaneously the way Grid Search or Random Search can, since both of those simpler approaches choose every combination to evaluate ahead of time, entirely independent of one another, making them naturally, easily distributable across parallel computing resources. This is a real, genuine practical tradeoff against Bayesian Optimization's sample-efficiency advantage, one worth weighing directly against whatever parallel computing resources are actually available for a given tuning task.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Some practical Bayesian Optimization implementations do offer limited batch or parallel variants, evaluating several candidate points simultaneously per round rather than strictly one at a time, but even these retain meaningfully less parallelism than the fully independent evaluations Grid Search and Random Search naturally allow.

blocks.text: 9. When Bayesian Optimization Earns Its Added Complexity

Bayesian Optimization earns its genuinely added implementation complexity specifically when each individual evaluation is expensive, hours of training time being a common, realistic threshold, since sample efficiency then matters considerably more than raw parallelism, exactly the tradeoff already covered in the previous section.

It also fits well with a moderate number of hyperparameters, not an enormous, high-dimensional space, since the surrogate model needs a reasonable chance to actually learn the underlying relationship effectively from a limited number of real evaluations. When evaluations are instead cheap and fast, easy to run in the thousands across parallel computing resources, Random Search's comparative simplicity, and its natural, trivial parallelism, very often wins out in practice over Bayesian Optimization's more sophisticated but inherently sequential approach.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below runs Bayesian Optimization using scikit-optimize, directly comparing the number of evaluations needed against Random Search to reach a comparable result.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from skopt import BayesSearchCV
from skopt.space import Real
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 4))
y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] * 0.5 + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=200) > 0).astype(int)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

search_space = {
    'C': Real(0.01, 100, prior='log-uniform'),
    'gamma': Real(0.001, 10, prior='log-uniform'),
}

bayes_search = BayesSearchCV(
    SVC(kernel='rbf'), search_space,
    n_iter=15,  # far fewer evaluations than the 25 used for Random Search
    cv=5, random_state=42
)
bayes_search.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

print(f"Best combination found: {bayes_search.best_params_}")
print(f"Best cross validation score: {bayes_search.best_score_:.3f}")
print(f"Test set score: {bayes_search.score(X_test_scaled, y_test):.3f}")
print(f"Total evaluations used: {len(bayes_search.cv_results_['params'])}")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Bayesian Optimization uses the results of every past evaluation to intelligently choose where to sample next.
It builds a surrogate model, commonly a Gaussian Process, to cheaply approximate the expensive true hyperparameter-to-score relationship.
The surrogate provides both a predicted score and an uncertainty estimate at every point in the search space.
An acquisition function combines these into one ranking, balancing exploitation of promising regions against exploration of uncertain ones.
It often reaches comparably good results with dramatically fewer evaluations than Grid Search or Random Search.
Its sequential structure, each step depending on the last, makes it far harder to parallelize than those simpler approaches.
It earns its complexity when each evaluation is expensive and the hyperparameter count is moderate, not enormous.
Cheap, easily parallelized evaluations often still favor Random Search's simplicity over Bayesian Optimization's sophistication.
Next up: Optuna, a practical, widely used library implementing this same Bayesian-style optimization with additional efficiency techniques.
